subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Miranda: The Patchwork Moon
description: A micro-lesson that makes Miranda: The Patchwork Moon usable.

hook.text: Miranda is a tiny moon of Uranus with one of the most bizarre surfaces in the solar system—a jumble of mismatched terrains.

buildup.text: It has enormous canyons 20 km deep, chevron-shaped ridges, and smooth plains all stitched together randomly.

discovery.text: Voyager 2 flew past in 1986 and captured images that stunned scientists. No one expected such a small moon to look so wild.

twist.text: One theory says Miranda was shattered by a collision and reassembled—pieces falling back together in a random patchwork.

climax.text: Another theory suggests tidal heating drove geological activity, pushing different icy materials to the surface.

punchline.text: A patchwork of cliffs and canyons. Shattered and reassembled, or heated from within.

quiz.question: What makes Miranda's surface so unusual?
options: It has mismatched terrains with enormous canyons, ridges, and plains stitched together randomly
It is perfectly smooth with no craters or surface features at all
It is covered in active volcanoes erupting liquid water

details.summary: Miranda, Uranus's smallest major moon at just 470 km across, has one of the most geologically bizarre surfaces in the solar system. It features enormous chevron-shaped formations (coronae), 20-km-high cliffs, and a patchwork of wildly different terrains — as if it were assembled from mismatched…
details.whyItMatters: Miranda shows that even small, cold moons can have dramatic geological histories. Its surface diversity challenges simple models of moon evolution and highlights the power of tidal heating to reshape worlds.
takeaways: Wildly varied surface with chevron formations and towering cliffs
One of the most geologically bizarre surfaces in the solar system
Tidal heating likely caused its extreme geological diversity

faq.question: What caused Miranda's bizarre surface?
faq.answer: Likely intense tidal heating when Miranda was in an orbital resonance with other Uranian moons (now broken). This drove internal convection that created the coronae — large regions of upwelling. An older hypothesis that Miranda was shattered and reassembled is no longer favored.

faq.question: How tall are Miranda's cliffs?
faq.answer: Verona Rupes, on Miranda's surface, is estimated at 5-20 km high — potentially the tallest cliff face in the solar system. Due to Miranda's weak gravity, falling from the top would take about 12 minutes, reaching only about 200 km/h. The cliff was observed by Voyager 2 during its 1986 flyby.
